findings: Current stable is Radicle 1.9.1 (built 2026-05-21, confirmed via files.radicle.dev releases manifest); the project moved domains in April 2026 — radicle.xyz now redirects to radicle.dev; radicle-httpd is separately versioned at 0.25.0.

Identity: rad auth creates an Ed25519 keypair under ~/.radicle/keys with a did:key DID that 'identifies your device'; every published artifact is signed; the CLI signs via ssh-agent (OpenSSH >= 9.1), with RAD_PASSPHRASE / --stdin documented as insecure bypasses; official docs state identities must not be shared across devices — the multi-device model is one DID per device, added as repository delegates via rad id update.

Repository identity: rad init mints a stable RID (rad:z...); the identity document at refs/rad/id carries delegates (DIDs), threshold, default branch, visibility, and optional canonical-reference rules; refs/rad/sigrefs self-certifies each node's published refs.

Issues: rad issue open/list/show/comment/edit/state/assign/label/react/delete; assignment targets DIDs; states are open/closed/solved; issue IDs are COB OIDs resolvable by unambiguous prefix; mutations announce to the network by default (--no-announce exists).

Patches: opened by pushing to the magic ref (git push rad HEAD:refs/patches; -o patch.message / patch.draft / patch.base push options); the patch ID is a COB OID; subsequent pushes to the auto-set upstream rad/patches/<id> create immutable revisions (force-push safe); anyone — not only the author — can publish a new revision; states are draft/open/archived/merged.

Review: rad patch review --accept | --reject --message, addressable to a specific revision, with hunk-level review via --patch/--hunk; rad patch show exposes each revision's base..head range for git range-diff (the narrative guide lags the CLI here; man page and source are authoritative).

Merging: there is no rad patch merge — a delegate merges with plain git (git merge patch/<id>) and pushes the default branch (git push rad main); Radicle detects the merged revision, marks the patch merged, and updates the canonical head; push output reports both.

Canonical state: each peer pushes only to its own namespace (the rad remote's push URL embeds the pusher's NID); the canonical branch is computed from delegate threshold agreement; canonical-reference rules (payload.xyz.radicle.crefs) can grant named DIDs — including non-delegates — authority over specific ref patterns.

Sync and verification: rad sync (--fetch/--announce, --replicas MIN, preferred-seed semantics) defines success by replication counts; rad sync status reports which nodes have replicated; push options -o sync / -o no-sync control waiting for network sync; Radicle is local-first — offline mutations propagate on reconnect, so durable-state verification must check replication, not local creation.

COBs: issues, patches, and identity are built-in COB types stored under refs/cobs/; rad cob list/log/show/create/update exists in 1.9.x, and create/update accepts arbitrary external reverse-domain type names with JSONL action streams (identity COBs excluded) — custom COBs are therefore possible in stock Radicle but have no high-level UX and no end-user documentation.

Automation: RAD_HOME selects the profile; headless operation is documented (RAD_PASSPHRASE with security caveat, systemd credentials, rad node events over the control socket, rad-<ext> PATH extensions); the HTTP API (radicle-httpd 0.25.0, apiVersion 6.1.0) is read-only — no authenticated mutation endpoints are advertised or documented.

Packaging: official install script (curl https://radicle.dev/install | sh) with signature verification, apt repo, AUR, and Nixpkgs; installs rad, git-remote-rad, radicle-node into ~/.radicle/bin; Linux musl and macOS builds; no Windows support.

Multiple profiles per machine use RAD_HOME (the seeder guide's dedicated-OS-user pattern is the official example); a second machine contributes either as its own delegate DID or as an ordinary peer pushing to its own namespace and opening patches.

Facts flagged UNCONFIRMED in official sources: ssh-agent socket forwarding practice; the non-delegate permission matrix for issue assignment/labels; hidden HTTP write endpoints (none advertised); external-COB validation semantics; concurrent multi-node single-host operation.
